title: One request. Two paths.
subtitle: Why does the API sometimes query the database, and sometimes skip it? Follow a request to see how a cache changes the execution path.
assumptions: A teaching model of a read API, not a performance measurement.
The cache-hit scenario assumes valid cached data. TTL, cache writes and error handling are outside this diagram.
Steps are sequential. Playback duration is presentation pacing, not latency.

scenarios.label: Cache hit - data already exists
scenarios.description: The cache contains the requested value. The API can respond without querying the database.

steps.title: The client sends a request
steps.detail: The client requests the product list. The API identifies the cache key.

steps.title: The API checks the cache
steps.detail: The API looks up the key before deciding whether to query the database.

steps.title: The cache returns a value
steps.detail: The key exists and is assumed valid. The API uses this value and skips the database path.

steps.title: Return the response
steps.detail: The API sends 200 OK. Switch to Cache miss to see the additional messages.

scenarios.label: Cache miss - read the database
scenarios.description: The cache has no value. The API must retrieve the data from the database.

steps.title: The same request arrives
steps.detail: The client still sends GET /products. The difference is the cache contents.

steps.title: The API checks the cache
steps.detail: The same key is looked up. No database query has been made yet.

steps.title: The cache reports a miss
steps.detail: The lookup returns not found. A cache miss is not necessarily a system error.

steps.title: Query the database
steps.detail: Without a cached value, the API reads the primary data source.

steps.title: The database returns rows
steps.detail: The database returns product rows. Cache population is outside this teaching model.

steps.title: Complete the request
steps.detail: The client receives 200 OK, after two additional messages to and from the database.
